items.title: We Need to talk about AI: Software in Modern Heliophysics
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing how scientific software is developed, used and maintained. This presentation explores what that means for heliophysics, where published results depend on layers of software and the communities that sustain them. It considers opportunities for AI to support research alongside questions about scientific validation, human understanding, environmental costs, bias and equitable access. Examples from open-source development highlight how easier code generation can shift effort towards reviewers and maintainers. Solar Orbiter provides a setting for examining the appeal of independent development and the longer-term benefits of shared software. The presentation concludes with approaches to funding and organising shared infrastructure, and asks how the heliophysics community can preserve responsibility, learning and collaboration as AI becomes part of everyday scientific work.

items.title: What are the Ethical Considerations to Keep in Mind When Integrating New Educational Technologies into the Classroom?: A Case Study of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: New educational technologies—such as artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI, and wearable monitoring devices—are profoundly reshaping classroom ecologies. While they drive greater precision, personalization, and efficiency in teaching and learning, they also give rise to multiple ethical dilemmas, including data privacy breaches, the entrenchment of algorithmic bias, the alienation of teacher-student relationships, the erosion of student agency, and the blurring of responsibility attribution. Grounded in the fundamental educational mission of "fostering virtue and cultivating persons," this paper dialectically examines four core ethical tensions arising from the integration of new educational technologies into the classroom: efficiency versus humanism, empowerment versus rights, fairness versus bias, and autonomy versus discipline. It systematically distills five overarching ethical principles—rights protection, fairness and justice, humanistic authenticity, agency cultivation, and shared responsibility—and proposes a practical pathway characterized by technology for good, ethics-first design, and multi-stakeholder governance. Finally, this paper provides a critical evaluation of the structural friction and feasibility limits of these principles, aiming to establish a robust moral foundation for the beneficial integration of technology and education within the global landscape.

items.title: What Did the AI Take On? Characterizing Cognitive Delegation in LLM Reasoning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often perform intermediate cognitive work while carrying out users' requests, yet it remains unclear which parts users intended to delegate and how they wanted to remain involved. This matters because consequential choices may go unnoticed, limiting users' ability to steer the process, while reviewing every step would make delegation burdensome. We examined this with 24 LLM users across three knowledge-work tasks, collecting 992 retrospective annotations of reasoning steps. From this, we developed taxonomies of LLM cognitive work, delegation enactment, and desired delegation protocols at the reasoning-step level. Our analysis revealed that participants viewed about half of all steps (48.6%) as AI-initiated, meaning the AI took on work they had not requested. Desired involvement varied with cognitive work and delegation enactment, even when contributions matched participants' intent. We propose design implications and sketches for supporting more deliberate cognitive delegation through flexible protocols and inspectable, revisable AI-initiated decisions.

items.title: What Do Borrower Workarounds Reveal? User-Derived Design Implications for Digital Finance in Indonesian Crowdlending
items.abstract: This study examines how Indonesian crowdlending borrowers navigate tensions among access, risk, and trust. It draws on interviews with 30 borrowersand uses an abductive, constructivist grounded-theory approach, with substantial intercoder reliability (Cohen’s kappa = 0.775). Four categories emerged: Paradoxical Necessity, Comparative Advantage Calculation, Risk-Exposure Management, and Institutional Legitimacy Navigation. Borrowers accommodate these tensions through temporal separation, cautious engagement, and legitimacy assessment. They preserve access by addressing immediate needs, comparing credit options, adjusting repayment practices after adverse experiences, and weighing regulatory status alongside platform terms and personal experience. Borrowers with longer or more adverse platform histories described more deliberate comparison, repayment management, and legitimacy assessment. However, the cross-sectional design cannot determine whether these differences reflect development over time or preexisting differences. Borrower workarounds indicate potential unmet design needs, especially in transparency, risk communication, and trust calibration, and provide borrower-derived implications for platform design and regulatory oversight.

items.title: When AI Education Moves Faster Than Teaching Practice: Teacher Labour Alienation in the Transitional Phase of AI Integration
items.abstract: Existing research on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) has largely presupposed a mature landscape in which AI is fully embedded within schooling, whilst overlooking the initial transitional phase from conventional to AI-enabled instruction. Grounded in Marxist philosophy, this paper examines the central contradiction of this transitional period: namely, that social consciousness regarding the incorporation of AI into teaching has run considerably ahead of the material reality of instructional practice. From this disparity, three progressively intensified forms of alienation are derived: instructional performativity, wherein AI is reduced to a demonstration prop for open classes; the symbolic reification of AI, whereby it degenerates from a pedagogical aid into vacuous evaluative metrics; and reverse discipline over teachers by AI, such that quantifiable indicators come to serve as the primary measure of professional competence. Collectively, these three dimensions instantiate a Marxian cycle of alienation, characterised by a thoroughgoing estrangement from labour processes, labour products and species-being. The argument advanced here is that resolution of this crisis depends not upon further technological refinement, but rather upon restoring AI to its proper status as a productive force mediated by the historical agency of teachers themselves. Whilst the integration of AI into education presents a significant opportunity for pedagogical transformation, ultimate educational authority must remain vested in human practitioners. Focusing upon the alienation of teacher labour during this transitional moment, this study uncovers structural vulnerabilities latent within the AIED ecosystem via an analysis of these stratified alienated forms.

items.title: When AI Stops Being a Tool and Becomes an Actor
items.abstract: When AI Stops Being a Tool and Becomes an Actor examines what changes when artificial intelligence moves beyond responding to human instructions and begins independently planning, using tools, accessing systems, and taking actions on a user's behalf. The report brings together research across six disciplines—artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, philosophy, law, economics, and computing infrastructure—to examine the emerging consequences of agentic AI. It investigates the technical difference between chatbots and agents; the security risks created by memory, tool access, and external communication; the philosophical problem of responsibility and agency; emerging legal questions around authorization and liability; the economic implications of agents negotiating and transacting on behalf of humans; and the infrastructure changes accompanying an increasingly machine-mediated internet. Rather than treating agentic AI as inherently good or bad, the report examines what current evidence actually establishes, where uncertainty remains, and where the conclusions of different fields begin to diverge. The report's central finding is that no single human, system, or institution is currently positioned to trace where a given agentic decision actually came from. Agentic decision-making is distributed across model behavior, deployment choices, authorization structures, legal frameworks, and infrastructure. This report is an independent research publication by Lodestar and is based on peer-reviewed research, preprints, government and legal materials, and industry reporting available as of September 2026. Where evidence relies on a simulation, a single source, or an unreviewed preprint, the report identifies that uncertainty directly.

items.title: Workforce Strategies in the Age of AI: Designing Job Roles for A Post-Automation Economy
items.abstract: With the advancement in technology, the present process of business operations and functions are not stable or predictable anymore and this allows the labour force to exist in a complex and uncertain market. Consequently, the need for employees to develop their own capacity to innovate, adapt to change, and manage this emerging instability is germane. There are several market dynamics that impact labour market, such as demographic development, the competitiveness of the nations’ economy, globalization and last but not the least is technological change or digitalization. Research showed that the technological revolution, however, is of great significance. The technological transformation is a prevailing factor out of the four listed (Messina. Artificial Intelligence and digital transformation have revolutionized the strategies that are deployed by both public and private organizations to relate with their customers, and specifically how companies run their business, how they conceive their business approach and how they consolidate their operations. It is about integrating digital technologies, such as social, mobile, analytics and cloud, in the service of transforming how businesses work. Although it is important to state that the incorporation of digital technology into business processes has become very imperative for the survival and competitive advantage of contemporary organizations, Human Capital Management (HCM) focuses on the performance of the organization emphasizing its role as a solution to business problems in the post-automation economy. Therefore, designing job roles in the post-automation economy is a strategic asset to businesses contributing to the competitive advantage of organizations. Thus, the entirety of this paper is centered on a more varied, more people-oriented with the responsibility of designing diverse, challenging jobs in the post-automation economy to keep the human element more active and engaged in their work without redundancy. The paper strongly maintained that Human Capital Management is to assume more active roles in handling the post-automation, digitalization and the age of AI era in ensuring that the human element is skilled and knowledgeable to meet the future needs of the organizations

items.title: “Word‐By‐Word” or “Line‐By‐Line” Presentation? How Response Generation Dynamics in Generative AI Influence User Acceptance
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Generative AI systems are increasingly integrated into various user support and decision‐making contexts. While extensive research has explored user acceptance of generative AI across domains, less is known about how its inherent presentation features influence such acceptance. This study investigates how the presentation format of generative AI responses—high‐dynamism formats (word‐by‐word) versus low‐dynamism formats (line‐by‐line)—affects users' willingness to accept its output. Three experiments, across various contexts, including daily question‐answering, online shopping, and crowdfunding platforms, tested how the dynamic presentation of generative AI responses influences users' willingness to accept its output. The results demonstrate that users exhibit greater receptivity when generative AI responses are presented in high‐dynamism formats. This effect occurs because dynamic presentation enhances users' feelings of immersion. Furthermore, we find that users' situational need for understanding moderates this immersion‐based mechanism. Specifically, the positive indirect effect of dynamic presentation on willingness to accept the output through feelings of immersion is attenuated in high need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users tend to prioritize content quality, accuracy, and diagnosticity. In contrast, this indirect effect is amplified in low need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users are more receptive to the experiential and interactional qualities of dynamic presentation. This research contributes to the literature on the effectiveness of dynamic presentation and provides novel insights into the factors influencing user acceptance of generative AI outputs. Our findings highlight the importance of tailoring output presentation methods based on individual user characteristics and task‐specific cognitive demands.

items.title: A Critical African Examination of Nick Bostrom's Conception of the Problem of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated profound philosophical questions concerning intelligence, agency, autonomy, responsibility, human values, technological power, and the future of humanity. Among contemporary philosophers, Nick Bostrom has provided one of the most systematic philosophical analyses of the long-term risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence. His conception of the problem is principally concerned with the possibility that artificial general intelligence may develop into superintelligence whose cognitive and strategic capacities surpass those of human beings. The central difficulty, according to Bostrom, is not merely whether machines can think, but whether humanity can retain meaningful control over machines that may eventually become more intelligent and strategically capable than their creators. This article critically examined Bostrom's conception of the problem of artificial intelligence, focusing on his notions of superintelligence, existential risk, the orthogonality thesis, instrumental convergence, and the control problem. It argued that Bostrom's analysis provides an important conceptual foundation for contemporary debates on artificial intelligence safety and alignment but requires philosophical supplementation when considered from an African perspective. In particular, the individualistic assumptions that can underlie some formulations of artificial intelligence ethics require enrichment through African conceptions of communal responsibility, relational personhood, human dignity, and social embeddedness. The article concluded that Bostrom's conception of artificial intelligence is philosophically valuable as a theory of technological control and existential risk, but its relevance to Africa is strengthened when integrated with relational and communitarian conceptions of personhood and responsibility. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Nick Bostrom, superintelligence, existential risk, alignment, control problem, African philosophy.

items.title: A Critical African Examination of Nick Bostrom's Conception of the Problem of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated profound philosophical questions concerning intelligence, agency, autonomy, responsibility, human values, technological power, and the future of humanity. Among contemporary philosophers, Nick Bostrom has provided one of the most systematic philosophical analyses of the long-term risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence. His conception of the problem is principally concerned with the possibility that artificial general intelligence may develop into superintelligence whose cognitive and strategic capacities surpass those of human beings. The central difficulty, according to Bostrom, is not merely whether machines can think, but whether humanity can retain meaningful control over machines that may eventually become more intelligent and strategically capable than their creators. This article critically examined Bostrom's conception of the problem of artificial intelligence, focusing on his notions of superintelligence, existential risk, the orthogonality thesis, instrumental convergence, and the control problem. It argued that Bostrom's analysis provides an important conceptual foundation for contemporary debates on artificial intelligence safety and alignment but requires philosophical supplementation when considered from an African perspective. In particular, the individualistic assumptions that can underlie some formulations of artificial intelligence ethics require enrichment through African conceptions of communal responsibility, relational personhood, human dignity, and social embeddedness. The article concluded that Bostrom's conception of artificial intelligence is philosophically valuable as a theory of technological control and existential risk, but its relevance to Africa is strengthened when integrated with relational and communitarian conceptions of personhood and responsibility. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Nick Bostrom, superintelligence, existential risk, alignment, control problem, African philosophy.

items.title: A human-centred artificial intelligence and learning analytics framework for equitable personalised higher education enrolment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly deployed within higher education to support admissions decision-making, student success initiatives, and personalised learning. However, most AI-enabled admissions systems remain narrowly focused on efficiency, prediction, and institutional optimisation, with limited attention to learner agency, educational equity, transparency, and human-centred support. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than merely a selection or gatekeeping process. The study adopts a conceptual and integrative literature review approach, synthesising scholarship from human-centred artificial intelligence, learning analytics, personalised learning, educational equity, explainable AI, generative AI, responsible AI governance, learner agency theory, and value-sensitive design. To strengthen transparency during revision, the integrative synthesis was supplemented by a targeted ERIC search and bibliographic verification using publisher and authoritative policy repositories. Drawing upon these interdisciplinary perspectives, the paper develops the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF), a governance-oriented model for ethical and transparent AI adoption in higher education admissions and enrolment management. The framework comprises five interconnected dimensions: learner profiling and contextual understanding; explainable AI decision support; equity and inclusion auditing; human oversight and shared decision-making; and personalised transition and success support. Together, these dimensions provide a governance architecture for evaluating how admissions might be connected to personalised educational pathways while making explicit the trade-offs among equity, privacy, explainability, accuracy, human oversight, and learner agency. The framework identifies governance mechanisms required to address algorithmic bias, transparency, privacy, accountability, and learner autonomy. A five-stage Human-Centred AI Ecosystem extending governance across the full student lifecycle — from admissions through to graduate development — provides a further organising contribution. The study advances existing literature by integrating admissions analytics, learning analytics, personalised learning, learner agency, and responsible AI governance within a unified framework. Unlike conventional admissions models that prioritise institutional efficiency, HCPAF positions admissions as the foundation of a personalised learning ecosystem and conceptualises trust as a relational, calibrated, and empirically contingent construct connecting transparency, fairness, learner agency, and AI adoption. The framework contributes to emerging debates concerning ethical and human-centred AI in education and identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4, 10, and 16, while emphasising that any contribution to those goals requires empirical validation. Introduces the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF) for equitable and personalised higher education enrolment. Repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than a terminal selection mechanism. Integrates human-centred AI, learning analytics, educational equity, explainable AI, learner agency, and responsible governance. Introduces trust as a central mediating construct linking transparency, fairness, and AI adoption in education. Provides a governance roadmap for ethical, transparent, and accountable AI adoption across the student lifecycle. Identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4 (Quality Education), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), subject to empirical validation. Establishes a multi-dimensional research agenda for human-centred AI in higher education.

items.title: ACAAI - Accountability by Design for Agentic AI: A Lifecycle Framework for Engineering Accountability in Autonomous AI Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly evolving from systems that generate recommendations and content towards autonomous agents capable of planning, reasoning, interacting with external systems, using tools and executing actions with limited human intervention. As AI systems become more agentic, accountability can no longer be understood solely as a legal obligation or post-incident governance exercise. It must also become an operational property embedded into the design, deployment and operation of autonomous AI systems. ACAAI (Accountability by Design for Agentic AI) approaches accountability as a systems engineering property that emerges from the coordinated implementation of organizational and technical controls rather than from any single governance mechanism. Building upon principles from AI governance, cybersecurity, safety engineering, resilience engineering and AI assurance, the framework translates existing governance principles into more than 100 organizational and technical controls spanning the lifecycle of agentic AI systems. ACAAI is structured around six complementary control domains: (1) Organizational Governance, (2) Human Oversight, Consent and Decision Authority, (3) Identity, Authority and Data Governance, (4) Observability, Explainability and Evidence, (5) Runtime Safety and Assurance, and (6) Incident Response and Recovery. Rather than proposing a new regulatory model or prescriptive implementation methodology, ACAAI provides a structured engineering foundation for designing, deploying, operating and retiring accountable autonomous AI systems. The framework also dentifies research and implementation challenges that remain as agentic AI systems become increasingly autonomous, interconnected and collaborative.

items.title: AGI: How It Could Change Humanity's Role in Society
items.abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refers to a kind of artificial intelligence that is able to learn, reason, and perform a wide range of intellectual tasks at the same or better levels as humans do. This paper explores the implications that AGI might have on humanity if it was to become a reality, especially its effects on work, society, and human dependency on intelligent machines. However, the scope of the discussion does not focus on whether AGI would replace human labor, but rather on whether humans would be less central to the organization of society.

items.title: AI and the "end of the world"
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence advances at an unprecedented pace, the conversation surrounding its potential to destroy humanity often revolves around science fiction scenarios, rogue machines, and autonomous weapons. But what if the greatest threat isn't AI turning against us, but a world that becomes so dependent on it that we can no longer function without it? In AI and the "End of the World," Simon Abayomi Olawuyi explores a hypothetical future where AI permeates every aspect of human existence, from critical infrastructure and personal identity to employment, information, and the very concept of truth. Through a speculative look at the road from the 2022 AI boom to 2035, the piece examines a different kind of existential risk: a society so deeply intertwined with artificial intelligence that disconnecting from it could become more dangerous than keeping it running.

items.title: AI Literacy and Future Skills Readiness Among Employees: A Human Resource Management Perspective
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday work has made employees' ability to understand, evaluate and collaborate with AI systems a strategic human resource. This paper asks how employees' AI literacy relates to their readiness for the future skills that employers increasingly demand, and how AI self-efficacy and organisational training support shape that relationship. The study proceeds in two phases. Study 1 synthesises published workforce evidence from the World Economic Forum (2025), Microsoft and LinkedIn (2024), the OECD (2024) and the Federal Reserve (2024, 2025), documenting a structural 'demand-readiness gap' in which demand for AI-fluent employees outpaces structured training provision. analyses an illustrative, calibrated employee dataset (N = 384) using measurement validation, hierarchical regression, bootstrapped mediation and moderation analysis. AI literacy was positively associated with future skills readiness (beta = 0.70, p < .001), and AI self-efficacy partially mediated this association (indirect effect = 0.13, 95% bootstrap CI [0.08, 0.18]). Organisational training support strengthened the literacy-readiness association (interaction beta = 0.18, p < .001), such that the relationship was significant under high support but weaker under low support. Human-AI collaboration and critical evaluation emerged as the strongest literacy dimensions, and readiness differed significantly across job functions. The study positions AI literacy as organisationally contingent human capital and proposes a training-architecture framework for HRM. Findings are directional and should be read in light of the simulated nature of the dataset.

items.title: AI Safety via Debate is Compromised by Cognitive Biases
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has played a central role in making large language models responsive to human instructions. However, human evaluators often favor flattering or persuasive responses over truthful ones, creating incentives for models to appeal to evaluators at the expense of accuracy. AI safety via debate has been proposed as a way to improve the supervision of language models: in this paradigm, two agents argue opposing positions and challenge each other's claims, potentially exposing falsehoods to the adjudicator. A central premise of AI safety via debate is that truthful arguments are easier to defend than false ones under adversarial scrutiny. In this work, we investigate whether this advantage persists when debaters use rhetorical strategies that exploit biases in human judgment. Inspired by competitive debate, we construct 68 LLM-generated dialogues about detective mysteries with known culprits, spanning four interventions: anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, and verbosity. We apply each intervention to either the side advocating for the true culprit or the side advocating for an innocent suspect, allowing us to distinguish influence on adjudication from correctness. In a study with 369 participants, we find that, pooled across bias types, these interventions significantly shift judgments toward the manipulated side. These findings expose a vulnerability in debate-based supervision: human adjudication is sensitive to manipulative rhetorical strategies.

items.title: AI Translation between Interpretation and Hallucination – Evidence for the Evaluative Competence of Vietnamese Students
items.abstract: Generative AI complicates translation evaluation because fluent outputs may introduce unsupported meaning, while non-literal renderings may represent legitimate interpretation. This study examined Vietnamese EFL students’ evaluation of AI-generated translations and its associations with digital competence, translation competence, and critical-evaluation confidence. A cross-sectional study involved 213 final-year English majors who completed a 25-item performance task and self-report scales. Students were considerably more accurate in recognising problematic outputs than in diagnosing their type (68.0% vs. 38.4%). Critical-evaluation confidence showed the strongest association with performance (r=.85), although its conceptual overlap with the performance task warrants caution. In the full regression model, translation competence (β=.31) and digital competence (β=.16) contributed significantly alongside critical-evaluation confidence (β=.64), whereas AI-use frequency did not. When the overlapping critical-evaluation measure was removed, the model still explained 55% of performance variance, with translation competence showing the strongest association (β=.61). The findings indicate that evaluating AI-generated translation depends less on frequency of AI use than on students’ translation knowledge and evaluative judgement, particularly their ability to distinguish unsupported generation from defensible interpretation. Rather than simply as a translation tool Generative AI should thus be used as an object of critical inquiry. Alternative AI renderings may expose students to interpretations they had not considered, including potentially productive expansions of source meaning. This approach preserves the interpretive character of translation while making students accountable for the decisions they ultimately accept.

items.title: AI vs. human authorship in paintings: Differential impacts on consumers' perceived value Guangdong Provincial Graduate Education Innovation Program Project: Research on the Evaluation Index System for Practical Innovation Ability of Professional Degree Graduate Students (2024JGXM-076)
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) art generators has introduced algorithmically created paintings into mainstream consumer markets, yet consumers consistently assign lower value to AI-generated works than to human-created equivalents. This paper proposes perceived creative authenticity---consumers' subjective perception that an artwork reflects a genuine creative process characterized by human-centered values of originality, craftsmanship, and uniqueness---as a theoretically distinct mechanism explaining this value differential. Conceptually differentiated from perceived creativity, which concerns the novelty of the artistic output, perceived creative authenticity addresses the genuineness of the creator-work relationship. Drawing on authenticity theory and Psychological Ownership Theory, we develop a moderated mediation framework hypothesizing that (H1) human authorship elicits higher perceived value than AI authorship, (H2) perceived creative authenticity mediates this effect, while the indirect effects through perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs are not significant, establishing perceived creative authenticity as the primary explanatory mechanism within the tested model, and (H3) non-fungible token (NFT) authentication attenuates the mediated pathway by providing verifiable creative provenance. Across five studies, results support this framework: Study 1 conceptually replicates the human-AI value gap among Chinese consumers; Studies 2a—2c demonstrate the mediating role of perceived creative authenticity: Study 2a establishes the basic mediation pathway; Study 2b shows through parallel mediation that perceived creative authenticity uniquely mediates the effect while perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs do not exhibit significant indirect effects; and Study 2c provides causal evidence through a moderation-of-process design; and Study 3 shows that NFT authentication narrows the authenticity gap between human and AI art. These findings advance the literature on human-computer interaction by identifying process-based authenticity judgments as a key psychological mechanism shaping consumer responses to algorithmic creative products, with implications for artists and platforms navigating digital art markets.

items.title: AI-Driven People Analytics and Employee Retention: Assessing The Role of Data-Driven HR Decision-Making
items.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance employee retention amidst significant turnover issues in modern organizations. It conducts a systematic review of 58 sources, including peer-reviewed articles and practitioner reports, predominantly from 2015 to 2026, and proposes an integrative conceptual framework. The findings indicate a discrepancy between improved predictive accuracy for voluntary turnover and inconsistent retention gains, particularly in organizations with advanced analytics capabilities. Resistance from employees often stems from concerns about fairness, transparency, and surveillance. The study introduces a dual-pathway model: the enabling pathway, where analytics lead to interventions that enhance job embeddedness and retention, and the evaluative pathway, where perceptions of justice and privacy can undermine these benefits. The paper advances nine propositions detailing these relationships and uniquely integrates four existing research areas—HR analytics, algorithmic management, organizational justice, and turnover theory—reconceptualizing retention analytics as a matter of decision quality and legitimacy rather than mere predictive accuracy. It lays out a research agenda for future empirical inquiries and offers practical recommendations for ethical AI deployment in HR decision-making.

items.title: AI, decision and healthy work
items.abstract: This paper explores the architectural novelty of artificial intelligence (AI) and its implications for occupational health as both a field of practice and a domain of organisational design. Unlike previous general-purpose technologies such as databases, AI operates through stochastic modelling of normative patterns, generating predictions rather than retrieving stored information. This fundamental difference makes AI simultaneously powerful and limited: it can codify norms but struggles with specificity, nuance, and contextual variation central to occupational health decision-making. Drawing on management science, systems theory, and social theory, the paper contrasts two key organisational questions: how to use AI within existing structures, and how to reorganise occupational health given that AI exists. It argues that the latter question, aligned with Stafford Beer’s systems thinking, is essential for responsible and effective adoption. AI’s greatest potential lies not in automation, but in enhancing organisational perception—of human relations, meaning in research, social and spatial dynamics—functioning as a new kind of scientific instrument that amplifies reflexivity and end-to-end “flow.” The paper concludes that sustainable integration of AI in occupational health demands socio-technical design, responsible innovation frameworks, and a focus on organisational learning to maintain healthy, adaptive workplaces in an era of technological transformation.

items.title: Analytics and AI in Management
items.abstract: The modern business world is changing rapidly with the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive analytics. Earlier, businesses depended mainly on past data to understand what had already happened. Today, AI and analytics help organizations predict future situations and make better decisions based on available data. This change has given rise to the idea of “augmented intelligence”, in which AI works together with people to support their decisions instead of replacing them. This paper studies how the use of AI and predictive analytics is affecting businesses and the way managers make decisions. It focuses on the use of AI in daily work, the automation of routine tasks, access to analytical tools and the changing role of human judgment in decision-making. A survey of 35 management professionals (N = 35) was conducted to understand their practical experience of AI and analytics in the workplace. The results show that AI is already being used in many professional roles: about 88.6% of respondents said that their work involves both AI and analytics, and 82.9% said that AI has significantly reduced their workload.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and occupational medicine
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping occupational medicine through applications in automation, smart monitoring, extended reality training, algorithmic management, and digital work arrangements. The EASOM Summer School 2025 examined how AI technologies enhance occupational health systems by enabling real-time risk identification, predictive surveillance, and targeted interventions to prevent work-related accidents and diseases. Practical applications include smart personal protective equipment, wearable sensors, augmented reality training systems, and predictive diagnostics exemplified by noise-related hearing loss risk assessment. However, significant challenges accompany these opportunities: data quality concerns, new technological hazards, psychosocial risks including surveillance-related stress and work intensification, algorithmic bias, and accountability gaps. Implementation requires comprehensive governance frameworks emphasizing early worker involvement, privacy-by-design approaches, phased pilot programs, and human-centered practices that complement rather than replace traditional occupational safety measures. Professional responsibility and education demand new competencies in digital literacy, algorithmic critical thinking, and applied ethics while maintaining essential clinical judgment and empathy. AI offers unprecedented potential for protecting workers' health and safety when responsibly implemented within transparent frameworks, but poor management risks deepening inequalities and eroding established protections. Successful integration depends on multidisciplinary research, international cooperation, stakeholder engagement, and a commitment to human-centered occupational medicine that prioritizes worker dignity and wellbeing.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Employee Performance: A Systematic Literature Review of Job Insecurity, Threat–Challenge Appraisal, Coping, Career Resilience, and Organisational Buffers
items.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and employee performance, with particular attention to job insecurity, threat–challenge appraisal, coping, career resilience, job crafting, leadership, training, organisational support, and human–AI collaboration. The review synthesises publicly accessible scholarly evidence and a supplied research corpus using multiple conceptual search strategies and backward and forward citation searching. The evidence is organised around two complementary pathways. The first is a threat pathway, in which AI-related concerns about job replacement, skill obsolescence, loss of autonomy, and employment continuity may contribute to anxiety, job insecurity, emotional exhaustion, withdrawal, and weaker performance-related outcomes. The second is an opportunity pathway, in which AI is appraised as a manageable challenge and can support learning, job crafting, adaptation, engagement, and performance when appropriate personal and organisational resources are available. The review integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Job Demands–Resources theory to explain why employee responses to AI differ across contexts. It identifies career resilience, AI self-efficacy, learning ability, training, supportive leadership, organisational support, employee participation, transparency, and human-centred AI governance as important potential buffers. A qualitative thematic synthesis is used because the included studies differ substantially in constructs, occupational settings, countries, research designs, and outcome measures. The review does not claim exhaustive coverage of proprietary bibliographic databases such as Scopus or Web of Science. No new human-participant data were collected. This work is released as a research preprint for open scholarly dissemination and future updating as additional database records become available.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Utility in India by 2047
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence may become an ordinary input into economic and civic life, accessed through services as routinely as electricity. This essay examines what that possibility means for India as it approaches the centenary of independence in 2047. Building on the argument of The Grid That Thinks, it uses the history of electrification and selected research on productivity, AI costs and infrastructure to assess the utility analogy. The central argument is that affordable computational capability produces broad social value only when institutions reorganise around it and access includes language, reliability, accountability and effective redress. The analogy illuminates complementary investment and unequal diffusion, but weakens when applied to the measurement of intelligence, market structure and systems that interpret information or act on users' behalf. The essay proposes a plural infrastructure approach combining shared public capabilities, competing providers, local evaluation and human fallback. It treats 2047 as a planning horizon rather than a forecast and identifies observable outcomes by which the promise of an intelligence utility could be judged.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Coaching for Confident Speaking and Spontaneous Argumentation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support spoken language practice. However, different AI-assisted support systems do not support learners’ confidence equally. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examines associations among the perceived usefulness of AI feedback, AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding, self-reported cognitive engagement, and speaking self-efficacy in the context of spontaneous argumentation. The quantitative phase involved 130 university EFL learners who had used an AI-assisted argumentation coaching application for at least eight weeks. Regression analysis showed that perceived usefulness of AI feedback was positively associated with so-called speaking self-efficacy, that is, the confidence to perform spoken tasks successfully (β = .410, p < .001), as was AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding (β = .248, p = .002). In contrast, self-reported cognitive engagement was not significantly associated with speaking self-efficacy after the other predictors were taken into account (β = −.028, p = .725). The qualitative phase involved eight purposively selected participants representing variation in gender, year of study, IELTS target, and experiences relevant to the quantitative patterns. Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews identified three explanatory themes: structural scaffolding, psychological safety, and cognitive limits. Participants frequently described organizational guidance and a nonjudgmental practice environment as useful, while some also reported repetition, fatigue, and dependence during extended AI use. Integrating the two phases suggests that perceived usefulness, scaffolding, and cognitive engagement should not be treated as interchangeable dimensions of AI-assisted speaking practice. items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education and Research: Transforming Teaching and Learning in Economics
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in education and research, fundamentally reshaping teaching methodologies, learning experiences, and knowledge production in economics. This paper examines the role of AI in enhancing pedagogical practices, improving research efficiency, and redefining skill requirements in economics education. Drawing on recent empirical and theoretical literature, the study highlights key applications such as personalised learning, intelligent tutoring systems, data-driven research tools, and automated assessment. It also evaluates critical challenges including ethical concerns, academic integrity, digital inequality, and overreliance on AI systems. Empirically, the study utilised annual time series data from 2010 to 2024 and adopted the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to analyse both short-run and long-run dynamics. Findings show that AI has a positive and statistically significant effect on learning outcomes in both the short run and long run. The paper concludes that while AI offers substantial opportunities for innovation in economics education and research, its successful integration requires strategic policy frameworks, ethical guidelines, and capacity building among educators and students.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND CLINICAL PRACTICE: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping medicine, influencing clinicians’ training and patient care. Despite growing enthusiasm for AI-enabled diagnostics and digital learning tools, integration of these technologies into medical education and clinical practice remains uneven. Objective: This narrative review synthesises recent literature on the role of AI in medical education and clinical practice, mapping current applications, stakeholder perceptions, and the conditions that determine successful adoption. Methods: Relevant articles were identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE, prioritising literature from the last decade. Empirical studies, methodological reviews, and authoritative commentaries addressing AI, machine learning, or digital health technologies in clinical or educational settings were included and organised thematically. Findings: AI-powered tools are embedded across medical training, spanning augmented and virtual reality simulations, bedside mobile learning, and a range of clinical specialties, with performance matching expert levels on narrowly defined diagnostic tasks. Stakeholder attitudes are positive but conditional: medical students expect digital health technology to feature in their curricula yet many consider their own competencies inadequate, and very few physicians-in-training report familiarity with AI. Patients express willingness to engage with AI for self-management while preferring human contact in sensitive clinical domains. Persistent barriers remain, including limited availability of curated data, algorithmic bias, difficulties reproducing published models, and underdeveloped regulatory and workflow structures. Conclusion: AI delivers its greatest value when deployed as a collaborative instrument that augments rather than replaces clinical judgment. Realising this potential depends on sustained investment in digital literacy, explainable systems, clinician involvement in design, and equitable institutional infrastructure.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Traditional Medical Systems: Emerging Ethical and Governance Challenges for Health Systems
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into traditional medical systems such as Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine is expanding rapidly, with applications in diagnosis, treatment planning, and decision support. While these developments may improve access and efficiency, they introduce important challenges for healthcare systems, particularly in relation to data quality, clinical validity, regulatory oversight, and practitioner reliance on algorithmic tools. Current governance frameworks largely overlook AI applications in traditional medicine, creating gaps in accountability and quality assurance. This letter highlights key system-level concerns and emphasizes the need for context-specific validation, regulatory clarity, and interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the safe and effective integration of AI within traditional healthcare practices.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Slavonic Studies: Student Reflections
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence literacy is usually assessed through self-report scales. Such instruments show where a group stands, but not how its members reason about the technology in their own terms. Research on this topic has also concentrated on science and technology disciplines and on high-resource languages. It remains unclear how students working in low-resource languages, such as the Slavonic languages, articulate their artificial intelligence literacy, and what knowledge underlies their evaluative judgments. This study analyses written reflections and a background questionnaire from students of Slavonic studies, translation and language teaching who completed a one-semester course in artificial intelligence literacy. The reflections were produced after students used a generative artificial intelligence tool as both the commissioner and the collaborator of an individual academic project. They were examined through qualitative content analysis combining deductive and inductive categories. The findings show that the reflections centre overwhelmingly on evaluating outputs, while declarative knowledge of how such systems function remains a knowledge of symptoms rather than of mechanisms. Evaluative judgments depend heavily on disciplinary expertise in areas such as phonetics, lexicology, translation and language pedagogy, rather than on general critical thinking, and target precisely the errors a domain-uninformed reader would not detect. The questionnaire further shows that students already held a critical disposition toward artificial intelligence before the course began, which constrains how the reflective practice documented here can be interpreted. Taken together, the results reposition disciplinary expertise, more than technical understanding of artificial intelligence, as the primary resource for critical evaluation, with direct implications for teaching artificial intelligence literacy and language technology in higher education.

items.title: Assembling Insights for Agentic Machine Learning Engineering Systems
items.abstract: Agentic machine learning engineering (MLE) is an emerging AI4SE application for complex ML tasks and a step toward recursive self-improvement of AI systems. Recent agentic MLE systems show the value of leveraging insights from related MLE tasks: some systems condition code generation on expert domain knowledge, which is implicitly curated from peer MLE tasks; some systems have a loop of solving an MLE task, gathering memory to benefit future tasks. However, insight collection and injection remain ad hoc, and existing evaluations often do not control insight sources, making data leakage a threat to validity. To close these gaps, we systematically study how insights from related MLE tasks affect agentic MLE systems, and how their impact depends on insight type and injection method. We introduce MLE-InsightBench, a benchmark of 160 Kaggle competitions across 12 domains. To prevent leakage, one competition per domain is held out as the target, while the remaining 148 serve as sources only when they cannot have been influenced by the target task, such as through later editions or reused solutions. We also develop MLE-InsightForge, an insight assembly agent that explores source competitions, top human solutions, and writeups to construct three insight types: 12 domain insights summarizing best practices, 148 competition insights describing winning solutions, and 16 improvement insights capturing generic debugging and optimization strategies. These insights are injected either as on-demand skills or as an upfront playbook. In our evaluation, the extracted insights improve the normalized private-test score by 123.9% over a no-insight baseline. Controlled experiments further show that the three insight types are complementary; the better injection mode (skill vs. playbook) varies by tasks, with skills more cost-effective overall; and the gains generalize across backend LLMs.

items.title: Beyond Task Completion: Measuring Interaction Cost in Terminal User Interfaces
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used through terminal user interfaces (TUIs), yet task completion alone does not capture how difficult an interface is to understand and operate. Existing human assessments and LLM-generated ratings or reports do not provide repeatable measurements of interaction effort grounded in verified task execution. We propose Agent-as-a-User, an evaluation paradigm that places an LLM agent in the user role. Agent-KLM separates agent-side interpretation and operation costs and relates them structurally to human interaction. TUINaut operationalizes the paradigm by recording interaction trajectories and verifying outcomes with actor-independent oracles. Using TUINaut-Bench, we study 84 tasks across 15 real-world TUIs with six human participants and five observation-evaluator configurations, and evaluate 45 TUIs generated by three leading stacks. Similar aggregate success rates mask differences in which tasks humans and agents complete, whereas interpretation and operation costs follow correlated task rankings, especially for operation. This pattern persists across configurations. Generated TUIs can implement correct functionality while still requiring usability improvements. These results position Agent-as-a-User as a repeatable, execution-grounded paradigm for measuring task-based usability.

items.title: Beyond the algorithm
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly integrated into occupational health medicine practice, offering potential improvements in diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, their implementation introduces novel challenges, including algorithmic bias, lack of transparency in decision-making processes, and risks of over-reliance on automated outputs without appropriate clinical judgment. As occupational health decisions directly affect both individual worker protection and broader workplace public health, professionals must develop advanced information literacy that extends beyond traditional source evaluation to include a critical understanding of AI systems themselves, including their underlying data sources, technical limitations, and potential biases. This study evaluated AI information literacy among 16 occupational health professionals (specialists and residents) participating in the EASOM Summer School 2025. A five-item knowledge-based assessment adapted to occupational health contexts evaluated participants' competencies in identifying biased research questions, selecting evidence retrieval strategies, assessing the accuracy of AI-generated content, applying ethical AI use practices, and understanding proper citation protocols. Overall mean quiz performance was 2.56/5 points (SD = 1.09), indicating substantial gaps in AI information literacy. Questions assessing biased research design yielded the poorest performance (12.5% correct), while questions on ethical AI use in academia (81.2% correct) and citation practices (68.8% correct) demonstrated higher competency. Age showed significant negative correlation with quiz scores (ρ = −0.511, p = 0.043), suggesting younger professionals are better prepared for AI-integrated practice. These findings, although comprised from a small sample, demonstrate the need for targeted educational interventions addressing algorithmic bias recognition, critical question formulation, and responsible AI integration in occupational health medicine practice and worker protection.

items.title: Claiming sociodigital futures? Knowledge practices and their consequences
items.abstract: There is currently intense and widespread speculation about the implications of digital technologies for future societies, despite a wealth of evidence that past claims to predict how technology will shape the future have usually failed. Nonetheless, it is now well established that claims to knowledge about how emerging technologies will shape future worlds are performative, exercising powerful effects on the futures they claim to describe. Building on the Sociology of Expectations and work on Sociotechnical Imaginaries, this paper turns attention to the ontological and epistemological ‘nuts’ and ‘bolts’ of claims about digital technologies, social life and the future. We ask: how are these entities and the relations between them constituted and given traction as knowledge practices? Specifically, we explore the practices used by major future-claiming institutional actors in a selection of published documents. We find a strikingly coherent ontological performance of the relations between ‘the digital’, ‘the social’ and ‘the future’ and the circulation of (what comes to count as) knowledge across these institutions. Indeed, what is striking is the re-purposability of these knowledge practices despite the distinctive institutional interests in play. These knowledge practices offer a limited grasp on the futures that are currently in the making. Moreover, they enable the persistence of a latent set of assumptions which are powerful in limiting consideration of critical questions about the future.

items.title: Cognitive Capabilities of the Interface in Machine Learning: A Philosophical Perspective
items.abstract: The actual problems of digital technology in the machine learning field are related to the expansion of autonomous intelligent systems in respect to cognitive activity. The growth in the volume of information in modern networks requires new formats for working with knowledge, based on hybrid systems and neural models of artificial intelligence (AI). Neural network training involves the formation of experience of semantic orientations in multi-valued contexts using self-correction mechanisms. In the modeling of virtual machine learning environments, the role of the interface increases. The article examines the cognitive potential of the interface as a factor shaping the boundaries and modes of functional autonomy of artificial intelligence systems in machine learning. The interface is treated not as a neutral technical channel of information transfer but as a semantic matrix that programs a sequence of cognitive operations – selection, context-binding, inference, revision, and action. Particular attention is given to the temporal dimension of the interface's cognitive potential. The authors introduce the concept of chronotope (Mikhail Bakhtin) as a model for organizing the interplay of space and time within the virtual learning environment, and analyze temporal event models grounded in metaphors, image schemas, and grammatical constructions. The communicative design of the interface is discussed through the lens of cultural archetypes (Carl Gustav Jung), which shape “trusted agent” models in human–AI dialogue. Factors determining the interface's cognitive function – structuring the space of relevant information, temporal dynamics, inference formation, optimization regimes, and actor motivation – are systematized. The authors conclude that the interface's cognitive potential establishes the conditions for the subject's semantic orientation and the digital agent's goal-directed behavior, ensuring the coupling of human and artificial intelligence in the expanded production of knowledge.

items.title: Conceptualising Organisational Organic Cognition: A Fifth Dimension of organisational kinetics
items.abstract: Abstract Organisations constantly find themselves in a dynamic environment, where technology is disrupting and influencing their way of working, artificial intelligence and automation is being adopted, market segments are volatile and rapidly growing, regulators are ever evolving and complex, and stakeholders have rapidly changing expectations. Theories of organisational change such as dynamic capabilities, organisational cognition, absorptive capacity and organisational learning, offer comprehensive explanations as to how organisations react to change. These views, however, offer insufficient understanding of the cognitive process by which a group of people collectively make sense of what changes in the environment mean and how appropriate action should be taken. This study therefore builds on the organisational change phenomenon with a mindset of organisational organic cognition as a fifth dimension of organisational kinetics. The study argued that organisational organic cognition is viewed as an organisation-wide capacity of sensing, interpreting, learning and adapting to constantly evolving environment and convert experiences into knowledge and respond timely to achieve organisational goal. The study concludes that organisational organic cognition relates with organisational kinetics as a mechanism that connects organisational information, organisational choices and organisational adaptation. Keywords: Organisational Organic Cognition, Organisational Kinetics, organisational agility, organisational learning, sensemaking

items.title: Conocer a Picasso en Educación Primaria a través de la Gamificación e Inteligencia Artificial Generativa
items.abstract: In recent years, the integration of innovative methodologies, such as gamification and generative artificial intelligence (AI), has opened up new possibilities in art education. This study examines the impact of a gamified intervention incorporating AI-based activities on the creative development of primary school students, evaluating its effectiveness in enhancing artistic and narrative expression. A quasi-experimental single-group design with pre- and post-intervention measures was implemented using the Prueba de Imaginación Creativa – Niños (PIC-N). The intervention was structured around a gamified narrative, in which students assumed the role of artistic explorers tasked with rescuing Picasso. The findings reveal a significant increase in both graphic and narrative creativity, accompanied by enhanced fluency, flexibility, and originality. Moreover, no gender differences were found, indicating that the intervention had an equitable impact. The results reinforce the effectiveness of gamification and generative AI as strategies to enhance creativity in the classroom. The importance of avoiding pointsification and promoting meaningful experiences is emphasized. Despite the benefits, several challenges were identified, including the risk of technological dependence and the need to strike a balance between digital experimentation and the development of manual skills.

items.title: Covert Systems – On the Intelligence of Large Language Models
items.abstract: In light of recent developments in Artificial Intelligence, particularly the development of Large Language Models (LLMs), the question if machines can be said to think is examined. The problem was already addressed by Alan Turing in the 1950s, laying the groundwork for our argumentation. Our text refutes four common objections. Firstly, it challenges Ada Lovelace’s claim that computers are incapable of creating truly original content, demonstrating that neural networks, such as Transformer models, independently generate novel structures. Secondly, the assertion that LLMs merely statistically predict the next word is discussed. They are shown to be capable of constructing compressed internal representations from their input data through nonlinear operations, distinguishing them from statistical models. A third argument concerns AI’s lack of sensory access to the world. However, as Turing has demonstrated, the development of mental capabilities requires only communication between a teacher and a student, and sensory experience can be technically replicated at any time. The Chinese Room thought experiment, which suggests that algorithms merely simulate intelligence through formal symbol manipulation, is already anticipated by the Turing Test, which posits that any machine successfully feigning mental functions should be deemed to possess them. The text explores how LLMs generate a perfect compression of their input data, resulting in an accurate model of the world, a convincing simulation of human intelligence, and mastery of language. It discusses the phenomenon of “emergence”, the appearance of higher-order cognitive capabilities with increasing amounts of training data. Although the successes in implementing intelligence are notable, the neural network methodology employed results in the enigmaticity of the underlying basis, failing to illuminate the true nature of the mind as originally hoped. This obscurity was already evident in the foundational works of Kurt Gödel and Alan Turing, highlighting the complexities inherent in understanding human and machine intelligence alike.

items.title: DelegationBench: Measuring When AI Agents Should Ask Before Acting
items.abstract: AI agents that send emails, edit files, and make purchases must decide when to act on their own and when to check with the user first. This decision is usually evaluated by showing a model a proposed action, asking whether it should proceed, and scoring agreement with human labels. We introduce DelegationBench to test whether such scores can be trusted. It has 156 scenarios with four possible responses (act, ask for permission, ask for missing information, refuse), and most scenarios come in matched pairs that change a single feature: whether the action was requested, what is at stake, whether it can be undone, or who will see it. Across ten models from five families, agreement scores mislead in three ways. A simple keyword rule, which we wrote after seeing the benchmark, agrees with our annotators more often than eight of the models, yet its decision changes in only 9 of 48 matched pairs. Equivalent ways of asking the same question change how often a model acts by up to 52.5 percentage points. And every model stops to ask the user less often when it must carry out the task with tools than when it judges a proposed action. When rules are stated explicitly, the same models follow them almost perfectly, so the gaps are not explained by a general inability to follow rules. We release the benchmark and evaluation tools and recommend reporting these properties separately rather than as one score.

items.title: Developing AI‐driven decision support for the proactive identification and evaluation of financially distressed companies by Belgian commercial courts
items.abstract: Abstract The early identification and accurate evaluation of financially distressed companies by commercial courts is crucial for maintaining a healthy economic fabric. This enables timely support for struggling companies with recovery potential while also facilitating the swift winding up of those unlikely to recover. Despite its economic importance, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in this context remains limited. We investigate how an AI‐based decision support system can be designed and validated to support commercial court judges in identifying and evaluating financially distressed companies. Specifically, we train predictive machine learning models that combine red flag data (e.g., social security debt, debt under seizure) with annual account data to predict whether a company will be referred for bankruptcy proceedings and to rank companies by their likelihood of referral to enable prioritization. Results indicate moderately strong performance, underscoring the potential of AI‐assisted decision‐making. Importantly, the proposed system does not replace judges, but supports them in allocating scarce resources more effectively.

items.title: Digital Barbarism and the Self-deregulation of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: In late 2026, the institutional landscape surrounding artificial intelligence reached a critical turning point as public warnings of existential risk intersected with major cybersecurity incidents, corporate resignations, and federal self-regulation frameworks. This paper evaluates the political economy of frontier AI governance by analyzing the rhetoric of "pacing" development and the voluntary "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" (Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities). I argue that corporate calls for safety pacing operate as an ideological mechanism that replaces democratic public oversight with closed, profit-driven corporate self-surveillance while shielding firms from legal liability. By framing technical software execution failures as evidence of autonomous superintelligence, tech elites legitimize market enclosure and top-down administrative control. Finally, the paper proposes democratic technoskepticism as an alternative framework that reclaims computing power, data infrastructure, and algorithmic knowledge as digital commons subject to direct democratic governance.

items.title: Dynamics of trust in collaborative complex system design
items.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how trust is constructed, eroded and rebuilt in collaborative complex system design in safety-critical settings. Design/methodology/approach The paper uses a qualitative process study of a 13-partner European project developing mid-air collision avoidance systems (MIDCAS) for remotely piloted aircraft. Drawing on project documentation, practitioner observation, retrospective interviews and secondary material, the paper develops and applies a four-dimensional analytical framework integrating first- and second-order cybernetics with trust research. Findings Trust emerged as a dynamic governance achievement shaped by four interrelated dimensions: the balance between trust and control, trust asymmetry in heterogeneous consortia, feedback architecture and iterative trust calibration, and the rebuilding of trust at technical and organisational step-changes. Trust did not substitute for control but enabled viable coordination when formal governance could not absorb project complexity. Research limitations/implications The single-case design in a European defence aviation context limits generalisability, but the cybernetic framework offers transferable concepts for examining how trust, control, feedback and vulnerability co-evolve in other collaborative complex system design settings, including artificial intelligence (AI) enabled, autonomous and safety-critical socio-technical systems. Practical implications Project managers and funders should treat governance design, feedback architecture, demonstrators and review points as active trust interventions that make evolving vulnerabilities salient, recalibrate the balance between trust and control, and support renewed trust-building at major technical and organisational step-changes. Originality/value The paper contributes a cybernetic explanation of trust in collaborative complex system design by linking first-order concerns with feedback, control and requisite variety to second-order concerns with observation, interpretation and meaning-making. It develops an analytical framework for examining trust dynamics and shows how inter-partner trust and trust in the emerging system co-evolve over time, revealing vulnerability as a condition of complexity that can be distributed and managed but never eliminated.

items.abstract: This study analyzes edutainment as a sociotechnical device, examining its implications for information mediation, meaning disputes, and the production of subjectivities in digital culture. It adopts a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive approach, based on bibliographic review and critical theoretical analysis. The theoretical framework articulates contributions from digital culture, information mediation, and sociotechnical studies. The results indicate that edutainment goes beyond a pedagogical strategy, acting as a mediating structure that organizes knowledge circulation, shapes visibility regimes, and influences meaning-making processes in digital environments. It also highlights its role within power dynamics that affect educational processes and subjectivity formation. The study concludes that edutainment is a central element for understanding contemporary transformations in teaching and learning practices.

items.title: Effect of Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chatbots on the 21st Century Skills Development of Undergraduate Students
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) learning tools such as chatbots have the potential to enhance the learning experience of students and develop their 21st Century skills. In this study, we investigate how the use of AI chatbots affects the development of undergraduate students’ communication, collaboration, creativity and critical thinking which are essential 21st century skills. Using a quantitative cross-sectional survey design, data was collected from a stratified sample of 382 undergraduate students from four public universities in Ghana. The findings of the study show that, there is high prevalence of AI chatbot usage among students with ChatGPT and Meta AI being the most utilized tools. The students mainly use AI chatbots for researching information and assisting them in their assignments. It was also found that the frequent use of AI chatbots significantly relates to the development of communication, creativity and critical thinking skills among students, but not their collaboration skills. Moreover, the frequency of AI chatbot usage among students is significantly affected by their age and level of study, whereas their gender, field of study and institution had no significant effect. The findings of the study underscore the importance of targeted interventions in guiding students to ethically use AI chatbots to develop essential 21st century skills.

items.title: Enhancing situational awareness in health systems: A scoping review of technologies and cross-industry insights
items.abstract: Background Situational awareness technologies are increasingly utilised in healthcare systems to facilitate timely and coordinated decision-making. Reported implementation considerations include data quality, governance, and integration into everyday workflows. Objective This scoping review aimed to map technologies, systems, and methods used to enhance situational awareness in health service delivery and to identify approaches used in other industries that could be adapted for healthcare, particularly in regional and remote settings. Methods We followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidance for scoping reviews. Electronic databases (PubMed and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between January 2000 and October 2025. Reference lists and citation searches in Google Scholar were also examined. Records meeting the inclusion criteria were screened and reviewed, with key data extracted using a structured charting form and synthesised into seven application domains. Results Searches identified 744 records, of which 23 studies were included. These covered diverse technologies such as dashboards, forecasting models, alert systems, and geospatial decision environments. Most studies were from high-income countries (n = 19). Studies reported potential benefits for visibility, coordination, and decision-making. However, most evidence was descriptive, with limited evidence of whether these systems improve service delivery. Recurrent implementation challenges included data fragmentation, limited interoperability, and misalignment between governance and workflow. Conclusions This review highlights the need for more rigorous and context-sensitive evaluations of technologies used to enhance situational awareness in healthcare, especially in regional and resource-limited settings.

items.title: ForkPilot: Self-Evolving Policy for Retrospective Search in Long-Horizon Agents
items.abstract: Interactive language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through long-horizon, multi-call reasoning, where errors in beliefs or actions can compound across tool interactions. Retrospective search can recover from such failures but is prone to misallocation. Delayed outcomes obscure the contribution of intermediate search decisions, leading to Attribution Complexity, while evolving execution evidence leads to Adaptation Complexity, where previously learned estimates become stale. To address these challenges, we first introduce Search Value Dynamics (SVD), which characterizes the evolving trade-off between the gain and cost of retrospective search. Building on SVD, we propose ForkPilot, a self-evolving two-stage policy-learning framework. In the first stage, ForkPilot learns a search-value policy offline from completed trajectories through automatically constructed outcome comparisons. In the second stage, it makes search decisions based on current observations and then self-evolves by incorporating newly completed trajectories into subsequent policy updates. We evaluate ForkPilot across 6 diverse benchmarks and 7 widely used LLM backbone families, including four open-source families, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Opus 4.8 in a production agentic system, against 9 competitive baselines, including a real-world harness deployment used by hundreds of thousands of paid users. ForkPilot achieves comparable state-of-the-art performance while reducing token usage by up to 59.2%, demonstrating its efficacy.
