items.title: From Access to Realized Affordances: University Students' Generative AI Engagement across Linguistic and Sociotechnical Contexts
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university students' academic work, yet student engagement is often examined through adoption, frequency of use, or general perceptions, with less attention to how it is shaped by linguistic and sociotechnical conditions. This comparative qualitative study examines how university students access, incorporate, and evaluate GenAI across three contrasting higher education settings in China, Japan, and Mongolia. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 42 undergraduates from one university in each setting, and the data were analyzed through qualitative interpretation supported by co-occurrence network and correspondence analyses using KH Coder. Across the three samples, GenAI was incorporated into academic practices spanning exploration, production, and refinement. However, access pathways differed across the three contexts. Participants in China navigated between domestic and global GenAIs, those in Japan predominantly used global GenAIs through Japanese, and those in Mongolia more frequently shifted to English when Mongolian outputs were perceived as less satisfactory. During their use of GenAI, students evaluated its accuracy, privacy implications, potential for dependence, and effects on critical thinking. The findings suggest that technological access alone does not ensure equivalent educational usability across linguistic and sociotechnical contexts. Building on the empirical findings and the analytical perspectives, an empirically informed integrative framework is developed in which student GenAI engagement is understood as situated, mediated, enacted, and evaluated. The framework conceptualizes realized affordances as educational possibilities that become practically usable through the interplay of sociotechnical conditions, linguistic resources, academic practices, and evaluative judgments.

items.title: FROM HUMAN TO ALGORITHMS: Social and Legal Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Employment in India
items.abstract: "A machine can now hire a worker, rate a worker and remove a worker, but it cannot be asked why."Artificial intelligence is affecting Indian workers in two ways, and the law has dealt with only one of them.The first is job loss. The Economic Survey 2024-25, in its chapter "Labour in the AI Era: Crisis or Catalyst?",found that middle and lower-wage workers doing routine service jobs are most at risk. It warned that acountry with a surplus of labour cannot afford long periods of unemployment.The second is control. AI now screens job applicants, assigns work, rates performance and, on platforms,removes workers altogether. The four Labour Codes, in force from 21 November 2025, recognise gig andplatform workers for the first time and extend social security to them, a workforce NITI Aayog projectswill reach 23.5 million by 2029-30. But the Codes say nothing about the algorithm that decides what theseworkers earn.This article argues that this silence is built into the law, not accidental. Indian labour law assumes a humanemployer who can be asked to explain a decision. When software takes that employer's place, the workeris protected only when thrown out, never before. The article examines the Constitution, the Labour Codes,the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, andthen the State laws of Rajasthan, Karnataka and Telangana. Karnataka goes furthest, requiring writtenreasons and notice before removal, along with transparency and non-discrimination in automatedsystems.The article concludes that no new law is needed. The rule-making powers already available under theLabour Codes are enough to bring the required reform.

items.title: Functionalizing Intimacy? Technological Mediation and the Limits of Emotional Optimization A Review of Relationships 5.0: How AI, VR, and Robots Will Reshape Our Emotional Lives
items.abstract: This critical book review examines Elyakim Kislev’s Relationships 5.0: How AI, VR, and Robots Will Reshape Our Emotional Lives (2022), which argues that emerging technologies are transforming intimate relationships from human-centered bonds into modular, technologically mediated connections. Drawing on a historical-sociological framework, Kislev proposes a periodization of relational forms culminating in “Relationships 5.0,” where artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and robotics function not merely as communication tools but as active relational partners capable of fulfilling emotional, social, and even sexual needs. This review contends that, although the book provides an ambitious and accessible account of technological changes in emotional life, its analysis depends heavily on a functionalist and techno-determinist conception of intimacy. By reducing intimacy to discrete “relationship components” that can be optimized and delivered by technological systems, the book risks de-socializing intimate relationships and overlooking their embeddedness within power structures, inequality, and ethical obligations. items.title: Generative AI as a Learning Scaffold for Indonesia’s National Criminal Code
items.abstract: Indonesia’s National Criminal Code (Kitab Undang-Undang Hukum Pidana, KUHP), enacted through Law No. 1 of 2023, became effective on 2 January 2026, creating a new learning environment in which students must master recently operative statutory rules while generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is already embedded in everyday academic practice. This study examines the perceived pedagogical utility of GenAI for learning the KUHP among 82 university students studying in Jakarta who were surveyed during January-February 2026. A cross-sectional mixed-methods design combined ten five-point Likert items with three open-ended questions. Seven items measured AI-supported learning utility, two measured source-verification literacy, and one measured overall perceived effectiveness. The seven-item learning-utility scale showed high internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = .943) and a mean of 3.68 (SD = .76, 95% CI [3.51, 3.85]). Students rated AI most positively for explaining previously difficult KUHP provisions (M = 3.84), while ratings were lower for identifying the legally relevant provision in a case (M = 3.56) and strengthening legal argumentation (M = 3.57). Learning utility correlated strongly with overall perceived effectiveness (Spearman rho = .721, p < .001), as did verification literacy (rho = .755, p < .001). In an exploratory ordered-logit model, both standardized learning utility (OR = 6.54, p < .001) and verification literacy (OR = 8.84, p < .001) independently predicted higher overall effectiveness ratings after adjustment for semester group. Open-ended responses emphasized simplified understanding, case application, and faster information access, but also indicated the need for official-source verification. The findings support a bounded pedagogical role for GenAI: it is most defensible as a scaffold for explanation, examples, and formative feedback, not as a substitute for statutory reading or independent legal judgment.

items.title: Generative AI in Art and Design Education: Keeping the Human in the Creative Loop
items.abstract: Research on generative artificial intelligence in education reveals a persistent divergence between successful assisted performance and the development of independent knowledge, creative judgment, and transferable skill. Studies of art and design additionally identify opportunities for iterative exploration alongside concerns about visual fixation, uncertain authorship, and dependence on generated alternatives. These findings create an instructional problem: educators need to determine which creative decisions should remain with learners, which operations can receive bounded assistance, and which activities can be delegated without bypassing the intended learning. Existing scholarship addresses these questions through research on scaffolding, human-AI collaboration, assessment, and psychological ownership, but these contributions require closer integration within everyday studio practice. This article develops a Process-Centered AI Integration Framework for secondary and postsecondary art and design courses. The framework allocates tasks through three modes, protect, support, and delegate, according to learning objectives and demonstrated evaluative capability rather than the proportion of an artifact generated by AI. Six recursive phases connect intention formation, bounded assistance, comparison of alternatives, purposeful revision, human critique, and reflection with independent transfer. Parallel curricular applications, assessment criteria, and a reusable assignment planner specify retained decisions, appropriate AI roles, and concise evidence of learning. The model addresses the performance-learning distinction by making disciplinary reasoning observable across creative production while treating process ownership, product ownership, and achievement as related but distinct educational concerns.

items.title: Generative AI-Assisted Writing in Indonesian Language Education: A Systematic Literature Review of Process Pedagogy, Critical Literacy, and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly entered writing classrooms, yet its educational value depends on whether it supports or bypasses the intellectual work of composing. This systematic literature review synthesizes 20 peer-reviewed international journal articles published between 2022 and 2025 to identify how GenAI, educational chatbots, digital multimodal composing, and critical digital literacy can inform Indonesian language education. A transparent search and screening protocol was applied to journal articles concerned with language learning, writing development, feedback, multimodal composition, authorship, equity, and academic integrity. The thematic synthesis produced five findings. First, GenAI can assist brainstorming, genre modelling, language reformulation, and formative feedback, particularly when students remain responsible for planning and revision. Second, process-based designs are more educationally defensible than product substitution because they make decision making and authorship visible. Third, hallucination, bias, privacy, overdependence, and unreliable AI-detection systems require explicit critical AI literacy. Fourth, multimodal and narrative research indicates that technology should strengthen meaning, cultural voice, and audience awareness rather than reward surface polish. Fifth, equitable implementation requires flexible access, teacher mediation, and assessment that values evidence, reflection, and revision history. Based on these findings, the article proposes a five-stage HUMAN-AI writing cycle for Indonesian language classrooms: human grounding, purposeful prompting, evidence checking, authorial reconstruction, and reflective disclosure. The framework positions GenAI as a supervised dialogic resource, not a substitute author.

items.title: Generative AI, Technology and the Ecology of Persistence: A Response to Tække
items.abstract: Jesper Tække's (2026) article addresses a genuine conceptual problem.Rather than treating generative AI as either a continuation of deterministic technology or a newly autopoietic entity, he argues that it is better understood as a form of non-trivial technology whose stochastic operations destabilise causal predictability while remaining embedded in organisational decision structures.Generative AI thus appears as a 'transgression' of technology, not because it ceases to be technological, but because it no longer fits inherited expectations of stable and repeatable causal outcomes.That argument is sharp and necessary.Tække is right to return the debate to Luhmann's distinctions and to resist the tendency to move too quickly from complexity, recursion or internal state-dependence to full autopoietic status.This caution matters because recent discussions have taken different routes: Reichel (2011) conceptualises technology as a self-referential system, Wiesmüller (2023) stresses autonomous functioning within relational governance, and Simões (2026) proposes 'mixopoietic AI' as a hybrid taxonomy for AI governance.Against this background, our response is not an attempt to win the label 'autopoietic' for AI.The disagreement is therefore narrower, but also more precise, than a yes-or-no question about AI's autopoiesis.At the level of the model considered as artefact, we are close to Tække: Recursion, adaptation and stochasticity do not by themselves justify calling a generative model autopoietic.A model does not reproduce itself in the strict sense required by Maturana and Varela's account of living systems or by Luhmann's translation of autopoiesis into the domain of meaning and communication (Maturana and Varela 1980;Luhmann 1995).It depends on training corpora, infrastructure, maintenance, organisations, users, energy systems and legal arrangements that it does not generate.Taken in isolation, the model remains non-autopoietic.

items.title: Governing and Securing AI in Healthcare: A Data Governance and Cybersecurity Framework for Clinical and Administrative AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in clinical decision support, imaging, documentation, revenue-cycle operations, and patient communication, yet many healthcare organizations still govern it as ordinary software. That gap matters because healthcare AI inherits two risk profiles at once: the safety and equity risks of clinical tools and the confidentiality, integrity, and availability risks of systems that process protected health information (PHI). This white paper argues that AI in healthcare cannot be secured without first being governed through its data. It presents the Healthcare Data-first AI Governance and Security (H-DAGS) Framework, which links five pillars (govern and account; know and steward the data; secure the model, pipeline, and agents; validate and monitor; and operate, respond, and assure) to 33 control objectives across the AI lifecycle. Each control is anchored to a data governance capability such as cataloging, lineage, quality, metadata, or stewardship, and each produces a named evidence artifact. The paper maps the framework to the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules, ONC HTI-1 decision support transparency requirements, FDA guidance on AI-enabled device software functions and predetermined change control plans, the EU AI Act as amended in 2026, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, and World Health Organization guidance. It then defines an operating model and RACI, a workforce skills matrix grounded in the NICE Framework and the HHS 405(d) practices, a minimum viable conformity package for resource-constrained African health systems, and a phased implementation roadmap with metrics.

items.title: Governing and Securing AI in Healthcare: A Data Governance and Cybersecurity Framework for Clinical and Administrative AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in clinical decision support, imaging, documentation, revenue-cycle operations, and patient communication, yet many healthcare organizations still govern it as ordinary software. That gap matters because healthcare AI inherits two risk profiles at once: the safety and equity risks of clinical tools and the confidentiality, integrity, and availability risks of systems that process protected health information (PHI). This white paper argues that AI in healthcare cannot be secured without first being governed through its data. It presents the Healthcare Data-first AI Governance and Security (H-DAGS) Framework, which links five pillars (govern and account; know and steward the data; secure the model, pipeline, and agents; validate and monitor; and operate, respond, and assure) to 33 control objectives across the AI lifecycle. Each control is anchored to a data governance capability such as cataloging, lineage, quality, metadata, or stewardship, and each produces a named evidence artifact. The paper maps the framework to the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules, ONC HTI-1 decision support transparency requirements, FDA guidance on AI-enabled device software functions and predetermined change control plans, the EU AI Act as amended in 2026, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, and World Health Organization guidance. It then defines an operating model and RACI, a workforce skills matrix grounded in the NICE Framework and the HHS 405(d) practices, a minimum viable conformity package for resource-constrained African health systems, and a phased implementation roadmap with metrics.

items.title: Information-Processing Reallocation: A Theoretical Analysis and Conceptual Model
items.abstract: When a technological system begins to perform an information-processing function previously performed by people, execution has changed, but it does not follow that relationships among activities, coordination requirements, decision authority, or organizational structure have also changed. This theoretical paper develops a conceptual model of information-processing reallocation through a targeted comparative analysis of literature on organizational information processing, function allocation, delegation, interdependence, coordination, work design, and human–technology collaboration. Information-processing allocation (IPA) is defined as the distribution of information-processing functions between people and technologies at a given point in time, and information-processing reallocation (IPR) as change in that distribution over time. The analysis shows that the extent of reallocation alone does not identify the extent of relational change or the coordination required, and that technological execution can transform rather than simply reduce human work. The model yields one testable proposition: all else equal, reallocations that shift task interdependence toward a more reciprocal form increase the need for mutual adjustment during execution. The paper also specifies empirical criteria for identifying functions, reallocations, interdependencies, and coordination requirements in longitudinal and comparative studies. The model is intended to separate changes in execution from organizational consequences that require independent empirical verification.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial en la educación superior: uso y percepción del alumnado de periodismo
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into university settings has accelerated in recent years, particularly following the proliferation of generative AI (GAI). This development has led to a heightened discourse surrounding the implications of AI on journalism education. In this context, it is pertinent to examine how students incorporate these tools into their academic practices and how they perceive their integration into university education. The objective of this study was to examine the utilization and perception of AI among undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in journalism programs at the Complutense University of Madrid. Additionally, the study sought to identify training needs and ethical challenges associated with its incorporation into the curriculum. A mixed-methods design was adopted, combining an online questionnaire completed by 332 students with a focus group. The findings indicated a pervasive adoption of GAI, with ChatGPT emerging as the predominant academic support tool. However, the specific training offered by the faculty received a moderately low rating, as did the perceived expertise of the teaching staff. The highest scores were concentrated in the ethical dimension, particularly regarding issues related to bias, disinformation, privacy, and the need for human supervision. The findings indicated a discrepancy between the routine utilization of AI and its systematic incorporation into the curriculum, emphasizing the necessity for a progressive, cross-curricular, and critical approach to its integration.

items.title: International Organizations, Regions, and AI Governance Systems: An Interoperable Layered Governance Model
items.abstract: This article advances a policy and management proposal for Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems to ensure humans remain meaningfully in control of consequential AI-assisted decisions and actions. It reviews steps taken by international, regional, and national bodies to manage AI services and addresses the fragmented landscape of modern AI regulation. By evaluating existing frameworks, the article proposes an interoperable, risk-based "Layered Governance Model" in which responsibilities are allocated logically across the AI value chain. The proposal focuses primary attention on the upstream governance of providers of general-purpose and frontier AI models, establishing common controls at that layer to create a scalable safety baseline for downstream applications. Simultaneously, it delineates downstream safeguards covering permissions, context of use, human oversight, continuous monitoring, and incident response. While no single framework can eliminate illegal actions by bad actors, developing an internationally recognized management standard and regulatory architecture guards against risks that threaten the reputation, stability, and security of twenty-first-century AI technology.

items.title: Leadership Succession in Professional Service Firms
items.abstract: Succession planning is uniquely challenging for professional service firms. Unlike manufacturers, retailers, or most other types of companies, professional service firms place a premium on human capital. Value is created through professional expertise, client relationships, reputation, judgment, and institutional knowledge. Artificial intelligence adds a new layer to this challenge because it can augment knowledge capture, professional learning, talent assessment, and client service while also changing the capabilities expected of future leaders. In AI-enabled professional service firms, succession planning must therefore prepare successors not only to inherit roles and relationships but also to exercise human judgment, ethical responsibility, and critical oversight when working with intelligent systems.

items.title: Learning Machines: From the Automatic Teacher to Large Language Models
items.abstract: A reconstruction is offered of the genealogy of educational automation, personalisation, and epistemic agency. The contemporary debate on large language models in education often treats generative AI as an unprecedented rupture. Yet its promises of personalisation, immediate feedback, and relief from repetitive teaching belong to a longer history. This article reconstructs educational automation from Pressey and Skinner through cybernetics, computer-assisted instruction (CAI), and intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) to large language models. It advances three claims. Educational automation redistributes epistemic labour rather than expressing a linear increase in machine intelligence. Personalisation repeatedly depends on prior standardisation of objectives, knowledge, and evidence of learning. Generative AI introduces a discontinuity by producing the explanatory discourse through which understanding is ordinarily recognised. Bringing these claims together, the genealogy reveals how successful performance can become detached from the formation of judgement. Its critical force lies in examining this tension against educational commitments to developing learners’ capacities, while making the normative priority of epistemic agency explicit. The decisive question concerns how relations among learners, teachers, and machines enable subjects to direct inquiry, evaluate claims, and regulate their dependencies. This criterion remains relevant even if models exhibit limited forms of understanding: the competence of an assisting system does not establish the educational development of its user.

items.title: Look Before You Leap: Thermodynamic Arbitration of Parametric and Non-Parametric Knowledge in LLM Agents via Self-Regulating Memory Architectures
items.abstract: The architecture of modern LLMs consists of a profound cognitive polarization. LLMs possess implicit intuition encoded in their parameters, yet rely on a disconnected, explicit mechanism to access the outside world. Agentic frameworks have not bridged this gap; instead, models are often compelled into pathological "induced amnesia." Under the prevailing "Retrieve-Always" paradigm, agents must distrust their internal knowledge, making every user interaction a "tabula rasa" event that must be checked externally. This creates reflexive dependence that can be thermodynamically wasteful, cognitively fragile, and susceptible to irrelevant context. We propose a return to first principles, operationalizing the biological maxim "Look Before You Leap." We introduce MARTA (Metacognitive Adaptive Retrieval and Thought Architecture), a neuro-symbolic framework that bridges parametric and non-parametric knowledge. Rather than treating retrieval as mandatory, MARTA models it as a cost, taking the leap only when perceived internal inadequacy warrants external information. By allowing the agent to gauge the entropy of its own thoughts before acting, MARTA enables deliberative retrieval and uncertainty-aware decision making. Our approach suggests that giving agents the capacity for introspection can restore a more efficient balance between internal knowledge and external information.

items.title: Machine Learning for Learning Machines
items.abstract: This special issue explores the profound intersection of machine learning, language, and pedagogy, questioning the fundamental role of artificial intelligence in educational and linguistic coordination. Rooted in the age-old dream of combinatorial devices – echoing historical figures from Ramon Llull to Jorge Luis Borges – the collection investigates whether language and thought can be automated without appeals to meaning and reference. As generative AI becomes ubiquitous, we confront a landscape where machines train humans, write academic prose, and simulate understanding. This issue brings together philosophers of technology, linguists, and educational theorists to analyze this paradigm shift. It spans historical genealogies of educational automation, the cognitive potential of human-AI interfaces, and empirical studies on AI literacy and coaching, alongside critical examinations of AI detection systems and the capacity of machines to truly “think”. Furthermore, a dedicated subsection reflects on Borges’s 1937 essay “Ramon Llull’s Thinking Machine,” using this historical lens to dissect contemporary generative models. Taken together, the collected papers reveal an increasingly recursive relationship between machine learning and human learning, bringing questions of epistemic agency, disciplinary expertise, semantic judgement, and evaluative competence to the center of debates about what it means to learn in an age of generative AI. This issue frames these diverse contributions, charting a course through the promises and perils of the automated word.

items.title: Methodology for improving students' intellectual-communicative competence through artificial intelligence in inclusive education
items.abstract: The article examines a methodology for enhancing students’ intellectual-communicative competence in inclusive higher education through the pedagogically grounded use of artificial intelligence. Drawing on approaches to communicative competence, competency-based learning, Universal Design for Learning, and AI-assisted language education, intellectual-communicative competence is defined as an integrative ability to analyze information, formulate and justify a position, interact effectively in a foreign language, and regulate learning through reflection. A four-component structure is proposed, comprising motivational-axiological, cognitive-intellectual, communicative-activity, and reflective-regulatory components. The study substantiates a methodological cycle of “diagnosis – intellectualization – communication – feedback – reflection” and identifies conditions for its implementation in an inclusive environment, including personalization, differentiation, accessibility, critical verification of AI-generated responses, and teacher mediation. The article argues that artificial intelligence should function as a cognitive-communicative tool rather than a source of ready-made answers and concludes that the proposed model requires experimental validation in authentic educational settings.

items.title: Moderating Role of General Attitude Towards Artificial Intelligence in The Relationship Between Attitudes Towards Medical Error and Proactive Behavior
items.abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study is the investigation of the moderating role of general attitudes towards artificial intelligence in the relationship between medical error attitudes (causes of medical errors and medical error approaches) and proactive behaviour, within the context of social cognitive theory. Methodology: The study was conducted using a quantitative research approach. The study sample included 399 healthcare workers identified using convenience sampling. The research data were collected at two different points in time using a time-lagged data collection method; analyses were carried out after the data obtained from the two data collection processes were matched. Findings: The research found that both the causes of medical errors and medical error approaches have a positive and significant effect on proactive behaviour. Similarly, it was found that general attitudes towards artificial intelligence also have a positive effect on proactive behaviour. However, the results of the moderation analysis indicate that general attitudes towards artificial intelligence act as a moderator in the effect of the causes of medical errors and medical error approaches on proactive behaviour. Accordingly, it was determined that where general attitudes towards artificial intelligence are high, the positive effect of the causes of medical errors and medical error approaches on proactive behaviour is weakened. Originality: This study contributes to extending Social Cognitive Theory in the context of attitudes toward emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence in healthcare. The findings demonstrate that the influence of individual cognitive factors on behaviour differs across contexts and contribute to the literature by explaining the relationship between attitudes toward medical errors, general attitudes toward artificial intelligence, and the proactive behaviour of healthcare professionals.

items.title: Multidimensional engagement effects of generative AI adoption among minority ethnic international students in UK higher education
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has become a prevalent tool in higher education, yet little is known about how its use affects the learning experiences of minority‐ethnic international students (MEIS). Drawing on an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and a four‐strand engagement model, this quantitative study surveyed 273 MEIS across UK business schools and analysed the data with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS‐SEM). The findings suggest that performance expectancy, effort expectancy and social influence predicted intention, and facilitating conditions and intention were also positively associated with self‐reported GAI use frequency. GAI frequency positively predicted cognitive, behavioural, emotional and, most strongly, agentic engagement. Multigroup analysis revealed that female students showed stronger effects of effort expectancy, performance expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions on intention than males; low‐experience students were more sensitive to effort expectancy than high‐experience peers; and postgraduate students exhibited stronger facilitating conditions, performance expectancy and social influence effects than undergraduates. The study highlights both theoretical and practical implications by linking GAI adoption with multidimensional student engagement, with the strongest association observed for agentic engagement, and calls for equity‐focused policy, curriculum interventions and institutional support targeted at individual access gaps among MEIS. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic? Generative AI (GAI) technologies are increasingly used by students in higher education for learning support. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) has been widely applied to examine technology adoption in educational contexts. What this paper adds? It extends UTAUT to an under‐researched population (MEIS), who often face heightened academic, technological and cultural challenges in UK higher education. GAI use by MEIS is strongly associated with cognitive, behavioural, emotional and especially agentic engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy Institutions should consider embedding GAI literacy and access support into orientation and academic skills programmes for MEIS. Educators who integrate GAI into teaching may consider structured questioning, verification and reflection activities while evaluating rather than assuming their effects on engagement. Policymakers should develop equity‐oriented strategies that support the digital and cultural integration of disadvantaged student groups.

items.title: NEOMANITAI: A Faceted Research Framework for Human-AI Interaction
items.abstract: This conceptual working paper develops NEOMANITAI as a research framework for describing human-AI interaction across digital, embodied and collective settings. It revises an existing umbrella proposal and distinguishes programme names, classification facets, concepts, observations and evidential claims. The edition presents eight ordering conventions, seven descriptive facets, a small typed relation model, three constructed civilian cases and four comparative research questions. The proposed contribution is an inspectable connection between programme navigation, episode descriptions and claim-level provenance. Its usefulness remains to be tested against simpler descriptions and existing approaches. The paper builds on selected historical programme documents and a targeted literature review covering distributed cognition, socio-technical systems, hybrid intelligence, collective intelligence, agents, human-robot interaction, conceptual work and taxonomy development. It reports no new participant data, empirical validation, global novelty finding or established disciplinary status. The constructed cases are explanatory examples. The English paper includes a German abstract. The accompanying JSON contains the conceptual model, examples and recorded literature reading scope. Files: paper PDF, paper TXT, model JSON, README and SHA-256 manifest. This is a new open-access edition. Earlier restricted source records remain separate and their access conditions are unchanged. Drafting and editorial checks were AI-assisted under the author's instruction; external peer review and personal sentence-by-sentence author review are not claimed.
